# Reranker Fragmentation: Why Your Single GEO Strategy Fails Across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude

## Introduction

If you’ve spent the last few years optimizing a single “Generative Engine Optimization” (GEO) playbook—one set of templates, structural markup, and content signals you assume will win across every conversational engine—you’re not alone. The idea that a single SEO-derived content strategy will reliably surface on every major LLM-driven answer engine is attractive: one set of assets, one set of KPIs, one budget. But the reality in late 2025 is different, and that reality is driven by reranker fragmentation.

Reranker fragmentation describes a technical and strategic splintering: different LLM platforms use different retrieval architectures, different reranking approaches, and different citation logics. Those differences mean a page that ranks well in Google—or that performs well in one LLM—may be invisible or de-prioritized in another. The divergence isn’t marginal. Empirical analyses show stark domain overlap differences between LLMs and Google, and reranker-specific models outperform generic LLM reranking by double-digit percentage points in relevance metrics. On the business side, LLM traffic behaves like high-intent referral traffic but with uneven conversion patterns depending on the platform that delivered it.

This post takes a technical look at why a single GEO strategy fails across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. We’ll unpack the architectural choices that drive citation and ranking fragmentation, walk through hard data on reranker performance and overlap with Google, and explain practical consequences for content teams and product managers. Along the way we’ll surface actionable takeaways: how to design a multi-platform content program, where to invest in specialized rerankers, and what to measure to avoid being “filtered out” before your content even reaches the model’s output window.

If you want to win visibility across multiple LLMs, you need to accept that “one-size-fits-all” is technically unsound. This technical analysis explains why—and gives you a blueprint for operating under fragmentation rather than hoping it disappears.

## Understanding Reranker Fragmentation

Reranker fragmentation stems from differences in three core system design choices: how sources are retrieved (search-integrated vs. pre-trained), how candidate documents are ranked (specialized reranker vs. LLM-internal scoring), and how the model decides what to cite and present within a constrained context window. The implications cascade through every stage of an LLM answer pipeline.

First, retrieval architectures. Some models (or model-driven products) integrate live web search as a primary retrieval mechanism. Others rely more heavily on dense retrieval from pre-trained corpora or proprietary indexes that were curated during model training. These choices shape which documents are even available to be reranked. For example, engines that search the web each query—Perplexity-style or ChatGPT instances using a search API—expose a broader set of up-to-date sources. Models that prefer pre-trained knowledge and selective retrieval expose a narrower domain set shaped by training data and curated retrieval signals.

Second, reranking approaches differ. A purpose-built reranker (a specialized model trained to score retrieval candidates for relevance) can significantly outperform a generalist LLM used as a reranker. Recent evaluations show specialized rerankers achieving higher NDCG@10 scores and doing so more cheaply and quickly than LLM rerank pipelines. That gap matters because when platforms choose where to invest—specialized rerankers, LLM reranking, or simpler lexical heuristics—the ranking surface the user sees changes.

Third, the citation logic varies. Models don’t just select the single highest-ranked document. They must decide which few documents to place into a context window that the model will actually reason over. Here the “lost in the middle” problem appears: when relevant information sits deep inside a long list of candidate documents, LLM performance on multi-document synthesis degrades. That drives many platforms to be aggressive in filtering candidate sets before the model sees them, privileging short lists of highly-curated sources.

The measurable consequences of those choices are striking. Analyses of LLM citation overlap with Google show ChatGPT had a median domain overlap with Google of only 10–15%, citing 1,503 shared domains that represented roughly 21% of its total cited domains, while URL-level matches were typically below 10%. Gemini showed even less overlap with Google in one analysis, sharing only 160 domains with Google even though those domains accounted for 28% of Gemini’s citations—representing just 4% of the domains in Google’s results for the same queries. Conversely, Perplexity’s search-integrated approach produced citation patterns more closely aligned with Google rankings. Those numbers are not a quirk; they reflect divergent architecture and curation philosophies that drive visibility outcomes.

Finally, there’s the economic and latency angle. Specialized rerankers are cheaper and faster. One provider’s reranker (`rerank-2.5`) reached NDCG@10 scores of 84.32%, outperforming major LLMs by more than 12 percentage points in head-to-head comparisons, while costing a fraction of the per-token price of LLM inference. These performance and cost characteristics affect which systems are practical at scale and therefore shape the ranking landscape you’re trying to optimize for.

In short: different retrievals, different reranks, different citation rules. The outputs diverge. A single GEO fails because it assumes a common ranking surface that does not exist.

## Key Components and Analysis

To operate under fragmentation you need to understand the key components that produce it and the quantitative evidence that proves it matters. Let’s break the system into the moving parts and the hard data that animates them.

1. Retrieval stage: lexical vs. dense vs. search API
- Lexical search (classic keyword matching) still returns useful candidates for relevance, but it often fails on semantic queries.
- Dense retrievers and search API integrations can locate semantically relevant documents, including fresh content not present in pretraining.
- Empirical evidence shows that systems using web search for every query (e.g., Perplexity) have citation patterns that map more closely to Google results.

2. Reranker stage: specialized models vs. general LLMs
- Specialized rerankers are trained specifically on relevance judgments and objective ranking metrics like NDCG. The result: better ranking fidelity and speed.
- Voyage AI’s reranker (`rerank-2.5`) achieved NDCG@10 of 84.32%, beating GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Qwen 3 32B by 12.61%, 13.43%, and 14.78%, respectively.
- Cost differences are large: specialized rerankers can be 25–60x cheaper compared with using a full LLM for reranking ($0.05 per 1M tokens vs. $1.25–$3 per 1M tokens). That pricing differential makes rerankers realistic for high-query-volume systems.

3. Context-window and “lost in the middle”
- LLMs degrade when many candidate documents are fed into the same context without proper prioritization. The “lost in the middle” effect can reduce synthesis accuracy.
- Two-stage retrieval architectures (first retrieve many, then rerank to a short ordered list) are effective because they prioritize the set the LLM will actually see.
- Example: rerank-2.5 improved NDCG@10 from 81.58% to 84.4% when reranking 50 documents after a strong first-stage retriever (`voyage-3-large`), but gains shrink or reverse if the candidate set grows too large (performance slightly declined when document count expanded to 200).

4. Interaction effects between stages
- The reranker’s marginal benefit depends on first-stage retriever strength. When the initial retrieval is strong, reranking yields modest gains (3.36% improvement with `voyage-3-large`). When initial retrieval is weak, reranking yields large gains (15.02% with `voyage-3-lite`, 47.57% with lexical).
- This interaction implies that end-to-end tuning—not isolated optimization—produces the best outcomes. It also explains why product teams that swap out only one component (e.g., put an LLM on top of a weak retriever) see unexpected regressions.

5. Platform citation patterns and overlap with Google
- ChatGPT’s median domain overlap with Google is only 10–15%, with 1,503 shared domains representing ~21% of ChatGPT’s cited domains. URL-level matches are typically below 10%.
- Gemini’s overlap can be even less consistent—only 160 domains were shared with Google in one study, even though those domains generated 28% of Gemini’s citations (representing just 4% of Google’s domains). That demonstrates Gemini’s selectivity or an independent citation model.
- Perplexity’s patterns align more closely with search-engine results because its pipeline integrates web search continuously.

These components yield two practical conclusions. First, the technical architecture determines what can be surfaced—optimization must be platform-aware. Second, cost and latency differences make specialized rerankers attractive operationally and strategically, and they are likely to be adopted where accuracy and scale matter.

## Practical Applications

With a clear model of why reranker fragmentation exists, let’s make this actionable. Here are practical ways to design content and retrieval systems that improve cross-platform visibility and business impact.

1. Treat each LLM as a separate distribution channel
- Build platform-specific visibility audits. For each LLM you care about (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity), measure domain and URL-level citation frequency for your core queries.
- Use those audits to prioritize where to invest: if Gemini rarely cites your domain for high-value queries, invest in Gemini-specific signal generation and validation rather than expanding an already-optimized Google footprint.

2. Invest selectively in specialized rerankers where you control the stack
- If your product relies on internal retrieval, use specialized rerankers rather than chaining an LLM to perform reranking. They’re faster, cheaper, and typically more accurate at producing the short candidate list the LLM can consume.
- Pair the best available first-stage retriever with a strong reranker. The biggest system-level gains come from balancing both components, not from replacing only one.

3. Optimize for citation eligibility, not just ranking
- Understand the heuristics each model uses to cite. Some engines favor authoritative canonical pages, others favor freshness or structured summaries.
- Make content machine-friendly for citation: canonical summaries, structured data snippets, well-labeled evidence sections, and clear provenance markers increase the chance a piece will be selected for citation rather than being deprioritized.

4. Shorten the path to the model’s context window
- Constrain your knowledge artifacts to present the most relevant evidence near the top. If an LLM has to synthesize from dozens of paragraphs, your facts can get “lost in the middle.” Use lead summaries, bullet-pointed evidence, and TL;DR boxes that map directly to likely prompts.

5. Segment content by intent and platform
- For Perplexity and search-aligned engines, prioritize freshness, ranking signals, and canonical SEO best practices.
- For ChatGPT and Gemini, add compact authoritative artifacts: executive summaries, clear source attributions, and well-structured Q&A pages, because these models are selective about what they cite.
- For Claude and other engines with different retrieval assumptions, run visibility tests and create targeted variants when necessary.

6. Measure platform ROI, not just impressions
- LLM traffic behaves like high-intent but unevenly converting traffic. Data shows mid-size companies (201–1000 employees, with 201–500 especially strong) generate the highest volume of qualified leads from LLM-sourced traffic. Track lead quality, conversion rates, and hiring segment performance by platform.
- Allocate budget according to where LLM-sourced leads are most lucrative, not just where you achieve the most citations.

These actions let you trade “one-size” simplicity for targeted efficiency—fewer wasted iterations, a more predictive pipeline for each platform, and improved conversion outcomes.

## Challenges and Solutions

Adapting to reranker fragmentation is not without friction. Here are the most pressing challenges and pragmatic solutions you can implement.

Challenge 1: Measurement and volatility
- LLMs and their retrieval stacks evolve quickly. A successful experiment can be invalidated by a model update.
Solution:
- Automate continuous measurement. Run daily or weekly controlled audits on a canonical set of queries. Use versioned baselines and record model details (engine version, retrieval architecture) with every test.

Challenge 2: Resource constraints and complexity
- Building platform-specific content and reranking pipelines increases operational complexity.
Solution:
- Prioritize platforms by business value. Start with a “big three” audit (Google-aligned search engines, ChatGPT, Gemini), and build minimal customizations first: canonical citations, structured evidence, and reranker-friendly summaries. Push heavier investments into platforms that deliver the best ROI metrics.

Challenge 3: Technical integration and cost
- Integrating specialized rerankers requires engineering effort; LLM-only reranking is tempting for simplicity.
Solution:
- Use hybrid approaches: offload coarse filtering to cheap lexical or dense retrieval, then use a small, efficient reranker to produce the short list. This reduces LLM usage while capturing most of the reranker benefit. Remember specialized rerankers are often 25–60x cheaper per token than LLM-based alternatives.

Challenge 4: Content discoverability vs. citation behavior
- Even well-ranked pages might not be cited due to model selectivity.
Solution:
- Make content citation-ready: include explicit evidence blocks, metadata with authoritativeness signals, and versioned timestamps. Use canonical pages for the same topic to reduce fragmentation within your own property.

Challenge 5: “Lost in the middle” on multi-document tasks
- Long candidate lists reduce answer quality.
Solution:
- Adopt two-stage retrieval with aggressive reranking to present the LLM with a tight, highly relevant set—50 or fewer documents in many cases. Benchmarks show reranking 50 documents improves NDCG significantly versus larger unranked sets.

These solutions won’t make fragmentation disappear, but they let you work with it pragmatically: measure frequently, prioritize ruthlessly, and use specialized rerankers where they move the needle most.

## Future Outlook

Where does reranker fragmentation head next? The technical and economic forces in 2025 point toward further specialization and pluralization of ranking systems over the near term.

- Increased adoption of specialized rerankers: Given significant accuracy and cost advantages, more production systems will adopt reranker components. As these rerankers become modular and accessible, platforms and enterprises that control retrieval will increasingly use them to improve answer accuracy while reducing LLM inference costs.

- Platform differentiation will deepen: Models will continue to refine distinct citation heuristics. Gemini, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude will evolve along different axes—some focusing on selective authoritative curation, others on up-to-the-minute search integration. That means platform-specific GEO will become par for the course.

- Measurement frameworks will mature: Standardized ways to audit LLM citation overlap and answer provenance will emerge, enabling better cross-platform benchmarking. Expect tooling that reports domain citation frequency, URL-level visibility, and lead-quality attribution by model.

- Business models will bifurcate: Companies that can control retrieval and rerank stacks will monetize higher-quality answers more effectively. Others will rely on partnerships or API-level agreements that expose less control and therefore less predictable visibility. The firms that own reranking capability get better accuracy at lower cost—an economic moat.

- UX and provenance norms will matter more: As users expect more transparent answers with citations, content that supplies clear provenance and structured evidence will have a persistent advantage. Models that are more selective will bias toward sources that make provenance explicit.

- Rapid iteration risk: The pace of model updates creates risk for planners. Strategies built on a specific engine version can become outdated. Continuous testing and an emphasis on platform-agnostic evidence design (clear authoritativeness, structured snippets) will reduce churn.

In short, fragmentation is likely to persist and even increase in the near term. The winning strategy is not to pretend the landscape is unified, but to build systems, content, and measurement that accept heterogeneity and exploit it strategically.

## Conclusion

If your GEO program assumes a single canonical surface across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and the rest, that assumption is increasingly invalid. Architectural choices made by each platform—whether to use live web search, how to rerank candidate documents, and how aggressively to curate citations—create materially different visibility outcomes. Empirical measurements underline the divergence: single-digit to low-double-digit domain overlap with Google for some LLMs, and double-digit gains in ranking accuracy when specialized rerankers are employed.

The practical takeaway is straightforward: design for fragmentation. Audit each platform, invest in specialized reranking where you control retrieval, make content citation-ready, and measure conversion and lead quality by model, not just impressions. Prioritize short candidate lists into LLMs to avoid being “lost in the middle,” and accept that some platforms may require bespoke content structures or canonical artifacts to be cited.

Reranker fragmentation is not a problem you can solve by wishful thinking—it’s a systems-level reality. But it is manageable. With disciplined measurement, targeted engineering, and content designed for machine citation, you can convert fragmentation from a visibility risk into a set of predictable channels that together drive better traffic, better leads, and better answers.
